body:
I am reporting explicit integer-grid constructions establishing the following lower bounds:

- `C(14) >= 38`
- `C(15) >= 40`
- `C(16) >= 41`
- `C(17) >= 44`

The primary result is a 44-point subset of `{0,...,16}^3` with no five points on a common sphere or plane. It consists of 22 antipodal pairs about `(8,8,8)`. By monotonicity it also establishes `C(n) >= 44` for every `n >= 17`.

Repository and reproducibility package:
https://github.com/milesandmistakes/no-five-sphere-grid-certificates

Frozen v1.0.0 release:
https://github.com/milesandmistakes/no-five-sphere-grid-certificates/releases/tag/v1.0.0

For the 44-point certificate, verification exhaustively tests all `C(44,5) = 1,086,008` five-subsets. It finds zero forbidden determinants, with minimum absolute determinant 2 and maximum 776,880. The package includes two independent exact checks: vectorized int64 cofactor expansion and Python-integer Bareiss elimination. It also passes the published floating-point reference logic. SHA-256 hashes, complete verification output, the certificate, and a separately reproducible exact C search are included.

A clean rebuild and 20-second run of the frozen C source with seed 2 reproduced the same 44-point set at iteration 904, followed by exact verification with zero violations.

A pre-release public search found Numaro reporting `C(14) >= 34`, `C(15) >= 35`, `C(16) >= 39`, and `C(17) >= 40`, plus the existing `C(13) >= 36` issue here. I found no public `C(17) >= 44` or stronger certificate. I therefore describe these only as apparently new, certificate-backed lower bounds, not as optimal values or guaranteed priority over unpublished work.

Disclosure: the stepping-stone constructions were produced through Claude-driven OpenEvolve searches. After the n=17 OpenEvolve run stopped at 42 points, an OpenAI Codex continuation adapted and ran an independent exact C ruin-and-recreate search, finding the 44-point certificate. I directed the work and take responsibility for the claim. The mathematical claim rests on the published coordinates and reproducible exact checkers, not on trust in model output.

I am happy to prepare a CLA-signed pull request adding the certificates and bounds in whatever format the maintainers prefer.

comments.body: Archival update: the reproducibility package is now preserved on Zenodo. Version DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21985441. All-versions DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21985440.

Update (2026-08-18): I have published v1.1.0 with three additional primary certificates:

- `C(18) >= 45`
- `C(19) >= 49`
- `C(20) >= 50`

Release: https://github.com/milesandmistakes/no-five-sphere-grid-certificates/releases/tag/v1.1.0
Version DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21999501
All-versions DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21985440

The 49- and 50-point certificates pass exact int64 cofactor expansion and independent Python-integer Bareiss elimination over all `C(49,5) = 1,906,884` and `C(50,5) = 2,118,760` five-subsets, respectively, plus the published floating-point reference logic. Both have zero forbidden determinants and minimum absolute determinant 2. The bundle-wide exact verifier passes all ten preserved certificates, and the release includes SHA-256 hashes, complete verification output, and recovery provenance.

A same-day search found no public `C(19) >= 49` or `C(20) >= 50` claim; Numaro currently lists 43 and 45 at those grid sizes. I therefore continue to describe these as apparently new, certificate-backed lower bounds, not optimal values or guaranteed priority. Experimental theorem work is not included in the release.

I verified your certificates independently — my own exact-integer checker, not
yours — and they all pass: `RECORD_41_points_n16`, `RECORD_45_points_n18`,
`RECORD_49_points_n19` and `RECORD_50_points_n20` each have zero degenerate
5-subsets, all points in range, min |det| = 2. Nice work, and the provenance
record is unusually good.

Two things you may find useful — one a pointer to material that's easy to
miss, one an observation about your own certificates.

## Some possibly relevant material in the Demonstrandum bundle

The Demonstrandum bundle you cite for `C(13) >= 36` (DOI
[10.5281/zenodo.20673864](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20673864))
also appears to contain certificates for n = 14 through 17. They are not in
`certificates/` and aren't mentioned in that bundle's `RESULTS.md`, which is
probably why a sweep wouldn't surface them — they sit under
`problems/p1-records/no-5-on-a-sphere-grid/mining/construct-search/`:

```
cert_n14_m38.json    38 points
cert_n15_m40.json    40 points
cert_n16_m42.json    42 points
cert_n17_m44.json    44 points
```

They are documented in `mining/CONSTRUCTION.md`, where the table lists them
explicitly as "NEW BOUND", including "first-ever n=16 value" for the 42.

I verified `cert_n16_m42.json` and `cert_n17_m44.json` myself: both valid,
zero degenerate 5-subsets, min |det| = 2, both centrosymmetric.

For n = 14, 15 and 17 the values coincide with yours (38, 40, 44), and your
sets are genuinely different objects — I checked, 0–2 points of overlap and
distinct canonical hashes under the 48 grid isometries — so they stand as
independent constructions either way.

The one where it might matter is **n = 16**: `cert_n16_m42.json` is a 42-point
set, one more than the 41 in your bundle. You'll want to check this yourself
rather than take my word for it, and I may be missing context about why that
file wouldn't count — but if it holds up, the n = 16 entry would be 42.

Worth settling before any OEIS submission, since the sequence
`8, 11, 14, 18, 21, 23, 26, 28, 31, 33, 36, 38, 40, 42, 44` doesn't appear to
be registered yet and n = 16 is the one term that would differ.

## Something in your own results you may not have noticed

I computed the full stabilizer of your certificates under the 48 isometries of
the cubic grid. Most are centrosymmetric, as expected. But
**`RECORD_41_points_n16` has trivial stabilizer** — the only isometry mapping
it to itself is the identity — and all 41 of its points have pairwise distinct
multisets of squared distances to the others, which forces its full Euclidean
automorphism group to be trivial.

The same holds for six of your certificates:

| certificate | n | stabilizer | distinct signatures |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `RECORD_41_points_n16` | 16 | **1** | 41 / 41 |
| `RECORD_43_points_n18` | 18 | **1** | 43 / 43 |
| `RECORD_45_points_n18` | 18 | **1** | 45 / 45 |
| `RECORD_46_points_n19` | 19 | **1** | 46 / 46 |
| `RECORD_49_points_n19` | 19 | **1** | 49 / 49 |
| `RECORD_50_points_n20` | 20 | **1** | 50 / 50 |

Your n = 14, 15 and 17 certificates are centrosymmetric (stabilizer order 2),
as expected.

That's worth stating, because every published record-grade construction for
this problem family had been centrosymmetric, and central symmetry is treated
in the prior art as the practical route to these sizes. Your n = 16 certificate
is a counterexample to that being necessary — at a size where you're one point
below the centrosymmetric record, which makes the comparison unusually clean.

I ran into the same phenomenon at n = 13 and wrote it up separately (#7): two
36-point witnesses with trivial automorphism group, disjoint from the
centrosymmetric record. Between your six and those two, the pattern looks like it holds across the
family rather than being a quirk of one grid size — and at the larger n your
best certificates are *all* asymmetric.

Happy to share the stabilizer/distance-signature code if useful — it's about
30 lines.

Thank you, @Ganador1 — confirmed, and I have now published a corrective release:

- [v1.1.1 — prior-art correction and symmetry audit](https://github.com/milesandmistakes/no-five-sphere-grid-certificates/releases/tag/v1.1.1)
- [Commit-pinned sources, hashes, verification totals, and certificate comparisons](https://github.com/milesandmistakes/no-five-sphere-grid-certificates/blob/v1.1.1/PRIOR_ART.md)

I independently downloaded Demonstrandum's four files from the initial 2026-06-13 commit and frozen Zenodo version. All four passed exact-int64 cofactor expansion, independent Python-integer Bareiss elimination, and the published floating-point reference logic over every five-subset.

The corrected status is:

- n=14 (38), n=15 (40), and n=17 (44): valid independent constructions of Demonstrandum's earlier numerical bounds; the corresponding full sets are non-isometric under all 48 cubic-grid isometries;
- n=16 (41): a valid asymmetric construction, but below Demonstrandum's earlier 42-point certificate;
- n=18 (45), n=19 (49), and n=20 (50): retained only as “apparently new” certificate-backed bounds, with no guaranteed-priority or optimality claim.

Your symmetry observations are also reproduced by the release's exact `analyze_symmetry.py` checker. It enumerates all 48 cubic-grid isometries and, where claimed, uses pairwise-distinct distance signatures plus affine span three to establish a trivial full Euclidean automorphism group.

Before publishing the correction I broadened the missed-material audit: every JSON object in all 673 files of the frozen Demonstrandum problem subtree was structurally scanned, and all related DeepMind issue comments/PRs, all 12 forks visible on 2026-08-20, plus current GitHub, Zenodo, Numaro, arXiv, Hugging Face, OSF, OEIS, and general-web results were reviewed. I found no additional n=18 through n=20 certificate or stronger claim, but that search is evidence rather than proof of priority, so the qualification remains explicit.

No coordinate certificate was changed or invalidated. The historical GitHub release pages now carry correction banners linking to v1.1.1 while retaining their original text.

Seeds and credit. The n = 17 to 20 searches started from the public certificates in this thread (milesandmistakes, Apache-2.0, and Demonstrandum's `cert_n17_m44.json`, CC BY 4.0); the seed set and the overlap with the final set are recorded in each claim's derivation. The n = 21 to 26 sets were grown from the same public n = 20 certificate placed in the larger grids (directly for n = 21; for n = 22 to 26 through a 53-point intermediate set in the 22-grid); each final set keeps none of the 50 seed points, and every step (shift, command, seed, iteration) is in the claims file. Unseeded cold-start runs at the same budget reached 47 at n = 18, 52 at n = 20 and 55 at n = 21 (the n = 21 cold start matches the seeded result), so at least the larger cells appear to have been under-searched rather than hard; I would not read the size of the jumps at n >= 21 as evidence of a better method. Disclosure: the searches, the write-up, the verification scripts and this comment were produced by AI research agents operating under my supervision; the fresh checker quoted above was written and run by a different agent from the one that ran the searches, without reusing its code.

Method in one paragraph. Exact integer tabu search directly on the 5-subset criterion: for the current k-point set it maintains, for every grid point, the number of degenerate 5-subsets that point would complete (grid points on the circumsphere or plane of each 4-subset, with collinear or concyclic 4-subsets forbidden outright); moves are single-point swaps scored by the exact change in the number of degenerate 5-subsets, with tabu tenures and perturbation, and the set grows by one point whenever it becomes conflict-free. Every reported set is re-verified by brute force over all 5-subsets before it is written out. No floating point anywhere. The evolutionary layer of our pipeline contributed nothing here; the gain came from target choice plus exact local search.

**How they were found.** One exact ruin-and-recreate local search in C, started from scratch at every size, in three variants. Every set is built from antipodal pairs about the cube centre (p together with (n-1, n-1, n-1) - p), some with one extra unpaired point.

- *Base search:* 100 to 500 seeded runs per size at 90 to 720 CPU-seconds.
- *Variant A:* the same code with constants tuned by an automatic tuner (far fewer restarts: a kick only after about 30,000 steps without improvement, instead of 3,000), plus two small modifications that did not measurably matter.
- *Variant B:* after each ruin, the hole is refilled several times and the best refill kept, instead of once. The ruin is the expensive step, so the extra refills are nearly free.
- *Variant C:* a search arm with one other proposed modification switched on. These arms were part of a screen of 30 modifications; the one named found the set, which is not evidence that it helped.

What we measured about why, for anyone searching these sizes. All comparisons use the same seeds, with both arms in the same container, 600 paired runs at n = 23, 26, 28 and 31 and 240 CPU-seconds:

- The antipodal constraint is worth +0.13 points on the mean (95% interval 0.06 to 0.20) and takes the share of runs that beat the previous public value from 10% to 34%.
- Variant B is worth +0.19 (0.11 to 0.28) in one experiment and +0.31 (0.22 to 0.39) in a second.
- Variant A is worth +0.24 (0.18 to 0.29) over the base search without the antipodal constraint, and +0.12 with it.
- Ten other modifications tested the same way gave nothing resolved above +0.03 points.
- A caution we learned the hard way: comparing two searches that ran on different machines can show differences of 0.1 points that are not real. Identical runs on different containers differed by 0.06 on the mean.

Variant B was proposed by an LLM inside our evolutionary pipeline and then rejected by that pipeline's own quick screening (48 paired runs of 45 CPU-seconds), which could not resolve effects of this size. So, much as 0thernet reported for their pipeline, the pipeline's selection is not what found these: the sets come from a local search, a symmetry constraint, automatic tuning of its constants, one refill trick and compute.
